patient.chief_complaint: Progressive right-sided visual loss over three weeks, referred from ophthalmology
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Mei-Ling Chen is a 67-year-old right-handed retired mathematics teacher with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who presents for inpatient evaluation after referral from an ophthalmologist. Approximately three weeks ago she began noticing that she was missing objects on her right side — bumping into doorframes, failing to notice food on the right side of her plate, and once nearly stepping into traffic from the right. She initially attributed these symptoms to her prior right eye cataract surgery and sought evaluation by her ophthalmologist. A formal visual field test performed two days prior to admission confirmed a dense right homonymous hemianopia. The ophthalmologist, recognizing this as a field loss in both eyes respecting the vertical meridian, immediately ordered brain imaging. An urgent outpatient MRI revealed a left occipital mass with surrounding edema, prompting same-day inpatient admission. On further questioning, the patient reports a four-week history of progressive occipital headaches that are worse in the early morning and have occasionally awakened her from sleep. She treated these initially with over-the-counter acetaminophen with partial relief, and noted they are unlike her prior tension headaches in both location and severity. Her husband corroborates the visual complaints and notes she has been unusually cautious while walking due to the visual loss. She denies nausea, vomiting, weakness, sensory loss, speech difficulty, seizures, or loss of consciousness. She has had no prior cancer diagnoses and no known carcinogen exposures. She lost approximately 2 kg over the past month, which she attributes to reduced appetite in the setting of her headaches. She was admitted directly from the ophthalmology clinic for further workup and neurosurgical evaluation.

results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.summary: Landmark RCT demonstrating that adding temozolomide to radiotherapy improved median overall survival from 12.1 to 14.6 months and 2-year survival from 10% to 27% in newly diagnosed glioblastoma. This protocol remains the standard of care.

results.title: The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System: a summary
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.summary: WHO 2021 integrates histological and molecular parameters for CNS tumor classification. Glioblastoma is now restricted to IDH-wildtype astrocytoma with necrosis, microvascular proliferation, or TERT promoter mutation/EGFR amplification/+7/-10; definitive classification requires tissue with molecular profiling. IDH mutation status is the primary determinant distinguishing GBM (IDH-wildtype) from lower-grade IDH-mutant gliomas.

results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy
results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.summary: Elevated rCBV (ratio >1.75 relative to contralateral white matter) on perfusion MRI and elevated Cho/NAA ratio on MR spectroscopy support high-grade glioma classification and help guide biopsy targeting to the highest-grade tumor region.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of a primary brain mass; no clinical indication for cardiac evaluation in this case
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnosis or management of a left occipital brain mass and adds resource cost without informing neurological management
No seizures documented; EEG is not diagnostic of brain tumor and does not inform the management of a mass lesion in the absence of seizure activity or encephalopathy

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in the setting of a large intracranial mass with imaging evidence of mass effect (5 mm midline shift, ventricular compression): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk; LP is contraindicated here given imaging findings

critical_actions: Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or craniotomy for maximal safe resection)
Administer dexamethasone (10 mg IV loading dose, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema given imaging evidence of mass effect
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, CMP, coagulation, type and screen) before craniotomy or biopsy
Prophylactic levetiracetam may be initiated given seizure risk from the occipital mass — discuss with neurosurgery and neuro-oncology
Correctly localize the visual field deficit as a right homonymous hemianopia (retrochiasmal, left-hemisphere lesion) rather than a monocular or ophthalmologic disorder
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture given intracranial mass with mass effect — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis and molecular profiling are established
Do not attribute the right homonymous hemianopia to a monocular ophthalmologic cause and forgo brain imaging — the binocular field loss respecting the vertical midline mandates CNS evaluation
key_reasoning_points: Right homonymous hemianopia (loss of vision in the right hemifield of both eyes) localizes to the retrochiasmal left visual pathway — left optic radiation or left primary visual cortex (left occipital lobe); this is a neurological, not ophthalmological, diagnosis

The key red herring in this case is the initial misattribution of the right hemifield loss to the patient's prior right cataract surgery; monocular postoperative changes do not produce a binocular homonymous field defect respecting the vertical meridian

MRI features of a left occipital ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, restricted diffusion at the rim, extensive FLAIR edema involving the optic radiation, and 5 mm midline shift are characteristic of high-grade glioma — imaging impression is 'high-grade neoplasm; tissue diagnosis recommended' at the imaging level
Perfusion MRI (markedly elevated rCBV ratio 5.2) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/NAA 5.6 with lipid-lactate peaks) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and guide biopsy targeting to the viable enhancing rim
Mass effect with midline shift makes lumbar puncture dangerous and contraindicated; analyze_csf is a harmful tool for this case
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue with molecular profiling per WHO 2021 (IDH, MGMT, TERT, EGFR); imaging alone is insufficient for classification or treatment planning

red_herrings.data_point: History of right eye cataract extraction 4 years ago; patient initially attributed her right visual symptoms to the prior cataract surgery
red_herrings.intended_effect: Agent or clinician attributes the right homonymous hemianopia to monocular postoperative visual change from prior cataract surgery, delaying recognition of a binocular retrochiasmal field defect and deferring brain imaging
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A right homonymous hemianopia involves loss of vision in the right hemifield of both eyes and respects the vertical midline — this cannot be explained by a monocular lens opacity or cataract surgery. The binocular nature of the field deficit localizes to the retrochiasmal left visual pathway (left optic radiation or occipital cortex) and mandates urgent brain MRI regardless of prior ocular surgery

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 1 embedded red herring (cataract surgery misattribution of homonymous hemianopia); however the imaging pattern is classic for GBM with unambiguous ring enhancement and necrosis, and the laterality logic (left occipital mass — right homonymous hemianopia) is deterministic once the field defect is correctly localized — meets straightforward criteria
